➡️From Vintage to MNTGE: Digital Fashion Brand to Release NFT Patches Linked to IRL Rewards

Digital fashion brand MNTGE is gearing up to release its Patchwork collection, comprised of a series of non-fungible token (NFT) patches paired with a physical counterpart.

MNTGE Patchwork features 13 unique digital patches designed by 11 artists including Jen Stark, Bored Ape Yacht Club artist Seneca and Nyan Cat meme creator Christopher Torres. The entire 7,500-unit collection will open for sale on July 27 on NFT marketplace OpenSea. Each NFT will be priced at 0.07 ETH, or $130, and the artwork will be revealed upon mint.

Each NFT is linked to an identical physical patch. Embedded with a near-field communication (NFC) chip, owners can scan the real-world patch to claim the digital token in their crypto wallet. By holding the patch on the blockchain and IRL, users can trace ownership as well as attend token-gated events and exclusive MNTGE experiences.

Additionally, the patches aren’t just one-off collectibles. In the physical world, they can be sewn onto MNTGE’s “base garments,” including t-shirts, jackets and denim. In the digital realm, the patches can be “owned” by the base garment itself. By implementing an ERC-6551 token standard, the digital wearable becomes a token-bound account that can custody the patches – creating an added layer of digital ownership.

Nick Adler, co-founder of MNTGE, told CoinDesk that the company was rooted in the goal of selling vintage fashion and utilizing the blockchain to revitalize its origins.

“People are out there wearing [vintage] and collecting it…young kids want to be authentic,” said Adler. “They don't want a Hot Topic shirt, they want the original shirt, right? So we just saw this natural, really honest use case for the blockchain, and we just felt like the two could really go hand in hand.”

📄 Iran-Pakistan border trade serves interests of both brotherly nations: Ambassador

📌 Islamabad, IRNA – Iran’s ambassador to Pakistan, Reza Amiri-Moghaddam, has described border trade between the two neighboring countries as an integral part of high-level bilateral agreements that serves the interests of both nations.

In a statement on Sunday, Amiri-Moghaddam, providing clarifications regarding reports of the closure of shared Iran-Pakistan borders, emphasized that any disruption at the borders, in the current circumstances, is neither logical nor in the interest of either side.
​
“There are currently no restrictions imposed by Iran on the export of Iranian goods—including Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG)—to Pakistan,” the ambassador explained, noting that “Iran’s borders with all neighboring countries remain open.”
​
Referring to problems arising for traders seeking to ship goods from Iran to Pakistan, he cited the implementation of the ‘E-Form’ procedure by the other side for imports from Iran, adding that consultations are currently underway to resolve this issue.
​
Amiri-Moghaddam also acknowledged reports that several hundred tankers carrying LPG had crossed the Gabd-Rimdan border into Pakistan, but said these trucks have yet to be unloaded or cleared—a situation complicating the movement of goods and disrupting the smooth flow of bilateral trade.
​
Emphasizing that cross-border trade serves the mutual interests of both countries and their peoples, the ambassador noted that Iran had spared no effort in facilitating and strengthening this vital bilateral commerce.
​
“We remain committed to continuing these efforts—in close coordination with our Pakistani counterparts—to overcome existing challenges, streamline the movement of goods, and further bolster economic cooperation between our two brotherly nations,” he underscored.
​
Meanwhile, Pakistani media also reported that the Gabd-Rimdan border crossing had resumed operations, and the flow of commercial transport has been restored on both sides of the border.
